content: before the bledisloe cup clash last saturday, nzr and movember teamed up to deliver ‘a moment against silence’, at eden park and on sky tv. it was a powerful reminder to check in on your mates, speak up if you're struggling, and stand with those facing tough times. today might be your moment. send a message. make a call. reach out to a friend, whānau member or one of the helplines below if you need support. let's break the silence. helplines you can reach out to for support: - 1737 (text or call) - youthline 0800 376 633 - suicide crisis line 0508 82 88 65 - aoake te rā (bereaved by suicide) 0800 000 053

content: it’s international women’s day. we reached out to some incredible wāhine making waves in their clubs and asked them for one piece of advice. their stories show what action, fairness, and belonging look like on and off the field. there is a place in rugby for everyone 💜
description_json: {"play_by_play": "Text screen: 'This International Women's Day we reached out to some incredible w\u0101hine making waves in their community and asked what their one piece of advice would be for any w\u0101hine wanting to get involved in the game.' Dee Clark (Manurewa RFC): 'Um, any advice I can give w\u0101hine in rugby spaces... Naku te rourou nau te rourou ka ora ai te iwi. Your basket and my basket, we will thrive. description_json: {"play_by_play": "So Heartland Rugby is made up of 12 provinces. Thames Valley at the top, East Coast, Poverty Bay, Whanganui, King Country, Wairarapa Bush, Horowhenua Kapiti, Buller, West Coast, Mid Canterbury, South Canterbury, and down the bottom, North Otago. So to be eligible for the New Zealand Heartland XV, players must play club rugby in one of those 12 provinces. They must play four games in a season. If you do that, then you're eligible to play Heartland rugby as a local player in the Heartland Championship. There's also players in our competition that are non-local. So each team's allowed four players from outside of that. Those players are not eligible to play Heartland XV. Some of the things that make Heartland Rugby special are the community connection to our players. content: 𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰: hear from neil barnes on his recent call up as all blacks senior assistant coach to take us through to the end of 2027 🫡
description_json:
{"play_by_play": "Interviewer: First question Barnsey, what does it mean to you and your family to be part of the All Blacks coaching group?
Neil Barnes: Oh mate, it's a huge honour and a massive challenge. It's not like I haven't thought about it as the responsibility that comes with the job. We're a country with high expectations. So, you ask me what it means? A lot. It hasn't sat easy with me shifting away from my province because I'm pretty passionate about my home place. But this is a new challenge and I'd really love to be involved in a team that makes this country proud.
Interviewer: Who were the first people that you shared the news with and what was that like?
Neil Barnes: To Megan. Yeah, I suppose we took it a little bit lightheartedly to start with, but it's really sunk in now. So, it's pretty moving. And yeah, it wasn't like it was a big announcement because you still have to be proven I guess by New Zealand Rugby Union and all that sort of thing, so yeah. It was moving.
Interviewer: Can you take us back to that moment you got the call from Rens? What was that like? What did you say to each other?
Neil Barnes: Look, I have to be honest there because when the opportunity came up, I messaged Rens to ask him if he was available to do the job because our country needed him to come back. I've worked with him before and I just honestly believe he's at another level. Yeah, and his reply back was 'Are you available?' and my message back to him was 'I don't think that's going to help you get the job.' [laughs] But then there was a bit more of an official phone call came when he was applying for the job as to whether I'd be involved in a serious manner. Yeah, very humbling. A lot of time for Rens. I guess there's a mutual respect there. But yeah, he's a challenging person to work with, but he gets the best out of people and teams.
Interviewer: What are the next few months look like for you as you step into this role?
Neil Barnes: Now we've got to really work hard. One to connect with our Super franchises and the players, and for me to get into the detail of the ability of all the players playing in that competition. Aside of that, Rens and I have had very long conversations about how we see the game. content: 🎥 dave rennie sits down for his first in-depth interview as all blacks head coach.
description_json:
{"play_by_play": "Interviewer: Dave Rennie, first of all, congratulations on your appointment. How does it feel to be the new All Blacks Head Coach?
Dave Rennie: Um, yeah, look, I'm really proud. It's a massive honour. I'm aware of the responsibility and expectations of the role and really looking forward to it.
Interviewer: Have you had a chance to speak to your family? I guess on a personal level this means a lot to you as well.
Dave Rennie: Yeah, yeah. They were the first people to find out, so the old group call and wake the wife up in Japan. A couple of my boys are policemen, so they had to sneak into another room to take a call that they normally wouldn't take on a weekday. So yeah, they were all really excited and proud and it was a really cool moment for us.
Interviewer: Obviously, there's something we want to acknowledge here, for me, I guess for a lot of us, that you are the first Pasifika All Blacks Head Coach, which is a massive milestone and a huge thing for Pasifika people, but also from a Cook Island heritage yourself, what does that mean to you?
Dave Rennie: Yeah, look, I'm really proud to be Cook Island Māori. My mum grew up in Titikaveka in Rarotonga, and you know, the best I reckon holiday paradise in the world. She's an amazing woman, really inspirational and had a massive impact on the lives of us kids, so I know she'll be looking down with pride today.
Interviewer: You're returning back home. What does that mean to you and your family as well to be relocated back to New Zealand and how does that feel?
Dave Rennie: Yeah, look, I'm rapt. I've been away a long time, been away nine years. You know, three in Scotland, three in Aussie, and three in Japan, and got five grandchildren, and yeah, so really looking forward to being able to spend a bit more time with them, and realize I'm going to be fairly busy as soon as I get home, but nice to be based back in New Zealand.
Interviewer: You've got a vast coaching experience across all different levels of rugby, I guess Tier 1, and you've got in different environments like you mentioned in Australia and Japan and Scotland. What has been the most valuable experiences that will help guide you in this All Blacks Head Coach role?
Dave Rennie: I think it's about people, like I've been lucky enough to work with fantastic people across the globe. I've learned a lot from that, and yeah, so I'm really clear on the way I want the All Blacks to play, the type of athlete we need to play that game, and have detail within that, so I think clarity creates confidence.
Interviewer: Your time with the Wallabies, I guess it's a Tier 1 team as well, how does that experience help you leading into this role?
Dave Rennie: Yeah, it's probably less scrutiny than in New Zealand. Half the country wouldn't realize there's a test match on, you know AFL fans or NRL fans, but look, I loved my time there. Again, I got to work with great people, I got to coach a lot of guys who I'd coached against at Super level and, you know, really good men and so I have no regrets, it was a really good part of my life being there. And sort of given me a little bit of experience around Tier 1 traveling and competing at the top level, so you know, I'm excited to have another crack at it.
Interviewer: 2026, it's shaping up to be a big year. When you look ahead at the schedule, what excites you most about it?
Dave Rennie: I mean, you've got to look at the first test, you can't look too far beyond that, so there's a hell of a lot of work to be done, some of it remotely over the next few months and make sure we hit the ground running against France. But you know, the tour to South Africa is exciting, well aware how tough it will be, but...
Interviewer: We talk a lot about coaching style. Do you have a particular coaching style that you want to bring into this environment?
Dave Rennie: Style... yeah, I'm probably the type of coach who gets an arm around people while I'm jabbing them in the ribs. Not sure how you describe that other than that, so... You know, I care about people. I think people want to know that you care, but you know, I'll also be driving them to be the best they can be.
Interviewer: I guess the question now is what happens from this point in, obviously confirming your coaching group and the transition from Japan, what does that look like?
Dave Rennie: You know, when there's a change of head coach, it affects a hell of a lot of people. You know, I've got people that I want to bring in who I think will make a difference here and yeah, but there's a process we need to go through, and so we'll probably have a bit more clarity over the next couple of weeks as to what all the support staff look like. Yeah, and then there's a hell of a lot of work to be done. The guys on the ground here in New Zealand will drive a lot of things in connection with Super Rugby and I'll come back every bye week to connect, and there'll be a hell of a lot of planning remotely, staff coming over to Japan so we can get a bit of work done there, so we'll try and maximize the time between now and July.
Interviewer: I know it's only been a couple hours since you were given the news, but what do you want fans to know as you head into this new chapter?
Dave Rennie: Yeah, look, I want them to know that I'll put together a group of people who will work extremely hard to make the country proud, and we've got a lot of talent here as we always have had, and so we certainly want to grow those guys and, you know, I guess everything's gearing towards a World Cup in '27, so yeah, excited about what we can do and what we can achieve.", "content_theme": ["player story"], "format_access": ["interview", "announcement"], "people": ["dave rennie"], "brands": ["adidas", "altrad", "toyota"], "event": ["all blacks", "world cup", "super rugby pacific"], "tone": ["pride", "excitement"], "context": ["announcement"], "overall_team": ["men"], "audio_format": ["voice"]}

As our numbers get lower on our jerseys then our time's elite might be 5:30 per se, six minutes per se for our props in our front row. The Bronco captures aerobic power, which is pretty crucial to the game. So if we want repetitive rugby actions in the game, our athletes have to have the ability to recover from those high bouts. So this helps us paint a picture of whether they can or cannot do that. If they can, awesome, we might spend our training time somewhere else in the week. If they can't, we might jump into the space a little bit across our training week. But ultimately, you know, with the way the game has been played around the world there's no excuse. This part of the game is key to speeding up your offense or slowing down on defense.

So, yeah, you're at water level and you're looking at this waka coming towards you, crashing through the waves or the currents or the river. The head is the tētē kura. Tētē kura was the front head of the waka that would crash through the waves and would make way for those that follow behind, or those in the waka. Inside throughout the jersey, you see manawa. They also represent players that have passed on, that have worn the jersey as well. But these chevrons here, or tāniko, also represent giving 100%, or providing 100%. content: what if training looked more like a game? we’ve partnered with the coaching gig to introduce game based coaching to provincial unions and coaches across the country 🏉 game based coaching keeps teenagers engaged in the game and coming back to play for longer.
description_json: {"play_by_play": "Matthew Stone (U15 Rugby Coach): 'So as a coach, we asked ourselves, what if training looked more like a game?' Coaches and young rugby players are seen practicing dynamic game-based drills on a rugby pitch with Mount Taranaki in the background. Matthew Stone: 'I've just seen a massive improvement in the players' engagement. For me, it's about how many touches of the ball they can have. If we're playing a game, there's multiple touches of the ball they have in short spaces of time, whereas in a drill or an activity where there's a queue, they might only get two or three touches within a few minutes. So that's the difference and you see huge engagement because they're always on the go, always touching the ball, and developing at the same time.' Ben Siffleet (Coach Lead - TRFU): 'Coaching Gig's awesome resource. I use it personally, I can plan my trainings on there, I can pull games out. Support for coaches through this game-based coaching trial through New Zealand Rugby has been awesome. I've really developed the game-based... whether with warm-up drills, whether it's games and activities, they've grown in confidence as they give it a go with support from the Coaching Gig myself.' Tom & Bryson (U15s Rugby Players): 'You got a good coach who gives you good tips and then you can kind of pick it up and then use it in the game. So much better than just... be getting out there, playing game, being active.' Matthew Stone: 'Game-based coaching is the way of the future. There's higher engagement in players, more touches of the ball, more enjoyment, and more growth in what they're learning on that training pitch.' content: what a journey 🖤 we can’t wait to see you back on the world stage @manaia.nuku! 🙌🏽 #blackferns7s | #svnsnyc
description_json:
{"play_by_play": "Producer: "If you could go back to the day after your injury in Hong Kong, what would you say to yourself?"
Manaia Nuku: "Everything's gonna be okay... Yeah. Everything's gonna be okay."
Commentary: "Oh, someone's slipped and gone down for New Zealand... That's Nuku, and she's in trouble."
Manaia Nuku: "It happened in the last 2 minutes of the game. I was quite disappointed, real sad. Um, felt like that was one of my best games that I've ever played, especially in a final, um, and then to go down like that. I didn't know exactly what I had done in the moment, but I knew it was bad. Probably about two hours later I was taken to the hospital and they ripped the Band-Aid off straight away, told me I had done my ACL. But even now, it's quite difficult to talk about cause I never wanna go through that ever again. First four weeks post-surgery, that was probably one of the hardest times. Uh, couldn't even bear any weight, couldn't walk. I needed assistance for a lot of things. To help support my recovery, I moved home with my parents. I think it helped take a lot of the pain away, and they brought a lot of joy into my life. I'm running today! Took my first steps. It was such a liberating feeling. For me, in that moment, the best thing in the world. Little moments like that reminded me you can come back and be a better player, better person than before. I just have to look back and be grateful for those moments now cause wouldn't have gotten to this place without all of those hard times along the way. I think as an athlete you can place a lot of your value into the sport, but for me it was figuring out my value away from it. I've always been studying, so I decided to take more papers, started another Bachelor in Te Reo Māori, then I also was studying a Bachelor of Sport and Exercise on the side of it. I also started coaching on the side. I also started an internship running content. That was good for me, like it helped clear my mind and give me something else to focus on. Looking back at it now, I think it was necessary in my development as a person, as a player. I guess everything works out. Man, it was probably the best feeling to see your number on the screen again. It's just pure joy and a lot of gratitude, a lot of gratitude. The biggest piece of advice I could give a younger athlete going through an injury is finding people that can help support you through this journey is probably one of my biggest bits of advice. What you see today, he was on size a lot different back then, but his heart was massive. Fearless, and just committed to go out there and really have fun and play the game that he enjoyed. Mason Malagamaali'i: Perhaps the one time that Ardie really jumped out at me was he was 14 and trialing for the under-16s Wellington under-16s program. And it was probably the first time where I thought to myself, and there was a handful of us thinking, goodness, there's a man amongst boys. And he was doing what we know now as Ardie things. Playing in the backline, then jumping into the forward pack. He was phenomenal, so we knew he'd go to great heights. Justin Gray: And that's, I suppose, what a lot of people don't see. Not just with Ardie, but with all professional athletes. They see the glamour on the Saturday at the stadium, in front of the lights. But they don't see the hours of hitting the gym, hitting the road, making good choices when it comes to diet. And that was, that's one of the sacrifices that I suppose one, if this is your goal, if this is your dream, that someone has to make for Ardie to do what he's been doing on the world stage for 100 games now. Poasa Poasa: It's awesome, and a lot of the kids in and around our community and our families look up to Ardie. Especially because he wears the same uniform as them. The black and white hoops is what they see. Mason Malagamaali'i: And when you hear Ma'a and Ardie talk about them now, they always credit their families, and especially their parents, because they've come from the generation of hard work. Growing up without a car, having to catch the bus or walk. It's quite a distance from Berhampore to Miramar, especially for rugby training and rugby games. Justin Gray: Well, I suppose the connection there is that he's quite a recent old boy. We still talk about Ma'a, Nonu... I mean, any boy in any code, in any field, that have gone through, we celebrate. We talk about, you know, the boys walking in the same corridors and sitting in the same desks that these boys have had. And it's a realization that, you know, a small boy that grew up in Berhampore had a dream, went out and grabbed it. Poasa Poasa: Yeah, that will be a really proud moment to see him put more honor, more grace, and more mana into his name and his family. Mason Malagamaali'i: But we appreciate him greatly. content: what a moment this was 🥹 🖤 chosen by the people of aotearoa, eroni clarke’s surprise anthem has been crowned new zealand’s sporting moment of the year 👏🏽 🎥: @skysportnz
description_json: {"play_by_play": "Caleb Clarke speaking on stage at an awards ceremony: 'My point of view of the whole thing... been a long journey to sort of get back into that black jersey, so I knew I was already going to be sort of emotional singing the anthem. And so, yeah, just having the eyes closed, hand on heart, got through the Maori part. And sort of when hearing the English part of the anthem, I was just like, man, this voice sounds so familiar. And throughout the whole thing, I had sort of Wallace on my left and Tamaiti on my right, both sort of patting me and then hugging me a lot tighter. And I just thought they could already see me crying, and they were like, 'Oh, that's all right, bro, welcome back, welcome back.' But there's sort of a moment there where I opened my eyes and I turn and look at the screen and see dad, see him singing the anthem real proudly. And I think, for me, I get emotional about it, just, you know, seeing dad who helped me throughout a low time throughout that year, sort of get back to the pinnacle of putting on the black jersey and looking to the corner and seeing him again sort of in that high moment. And so, yeah, just shows just the awesome thing about family and family support. So, yeah, it was real special.' Presenter: 'Caleb! Dear oh dear, that's too much. But you must be incredibly proud, and you seemed so proud when you were singing the anthem. But then the whole occasion, speaking to that, a sold-out Eden Park crowd, it was a very important match obviously, and then your son scores the opening try for the All Blacks. It must have been pretty surreal?' Eroni Clarke: 'Well, it's actually quite incredible. When I finished singing and I stepped down, and you just think, 'Ah, the job is done.' I just thought as I was walking off the field, just to turn to my right, because I hadn't seen him, we hadn't connected. And then as soon as he looked over and we kind of connected, we saw each other, and him running over to me, that just took us right out of that whole sporting environment. It took us into family and we embraced each other, and just that father-son thing was just incredible. And he said to me, 'Dad, you didn't tell me!' And I said, 'Of course! description_json: {"play_by_play": "As I finished the national anthem and stepped down from the mic stand and walking off the field, and I just thought to pause and have a look and just to kind of spot him where he might be as I knew they'd be going towards doing the haka. And the thought of that really put chills in my spine. But, so at the night before the South African Test at Eden Park, I went to the sound check, tried it, and when I did it, I just thought 'Okay, well, what... yeah, you're gonna ask me next year, or in a couple of years, or something like that.' And then in a matter of 48 hours, debuted and got called into the World Cup squad. It was so cool telling my family, so I got to call mum and dad straight away and let them know, and they were very excited, as you could imagine. I think it's massive, and I didn't realize how much it meant until I seen them on the field after my debut and how happy they were and knowing that they've been on the journey with me, the highs and the lows. There's a lot of physical strain with the Army, and then training for rugby at the same time. So being able to make sure I'm getting what I need to be fighting fit for the Army and then to be able to play rugby as well has been pretty challenging. They've been super supportive in terms of my work output and hours so that I can have the best of both worlds. And then when I got my contract, I had to make the decision to focus fully on rugby and take a break from the Army.
